newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will not waive immunity of envoy to Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will not waive immunity of envoy to Nigeria.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Thursday it had no intention of waiving the diplomatic immunity of the U.S. ambassador to Nigeria to enable him to be questioned about terrorist bombings there.
"Our ambassador is not going to give up his diplomatic immunity to appear at a hearing in a country that's dictatorial and that has no rule of law," department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"That would be foolhardy on our part, and it's not going to happen," Burns told a news briefing.

Nigerian police chief Inspector General Ibrahim Coomassie said on Tuesday he would require ambassador Walter Carrington's immunity to be waived to question him about a spate of bombings blamed on opponents of military ruler Gen. Sani Abacha.
The U.S. embassy in Lagos said on Wednesday it had not received a request to interrogate the ambassador.
Burns described Coomassie's statement as "very curious" and suggested there had been a misunderstanding.

"The Nigerians must have misunderstood either this issue, or they must have mis-stated something or mis-communicated their intentions publicly, because we cannot figure out what the Nigerians are up to," he said.
"To assert or to imply in any way that the United States is involved in terrorism in Nigeria is outrageous and unfounded," he added.
"So I think probably we ought to toss the ball back into the Nigerian court and ask them for an explanation of these very curious and unusual charges."

Politically-volatile Nigeria has been hit by a series of blasts since December, most of which have targeted military vehicles. The most recent, in May, killed five worshippers at a mosque in the eastern city of Onitsha.
Carrington has severely criticised Abacha's government for human rights abuses, especially the holding of political prisoners, and its programme to restore democracy by October 1998.
